# Objective
Fixes #1907. IO and Async Compute threads are sitting idle even when the compute threads are at capacity. This results in poor thread utilization.

## Solution
Move the distinction between compute, async compute, and IO threads out of userspace, and internalize the distinction into `TaskPool`. This creates three tiers of threads and tasks: one for each group. Higher priority tasks can run on lower priority threads, if and only if they're currently idle, but the lower priority threads will prioritize their specific workload over higher priority ones. Priority goes `compute > io > async compute`.

For example, heavy per-frame compute workload, async compute and IO otherwise sitting idle: compute tasks will be scheduled onto async compute and IO threads whenever idle. Any IO task that is awoken will take precedence over the compute tasks.

In another case, a heavy IO workload will schedule onto idle async compute threads, but will never use a compute thread. This prevents lower priority tasks from starving out higher priority tasks.

The priority scheme chosen assumes well-behaved scheduling that adheres to the following principles:

 - Compute tasks are latency sensitive and generally do not hold the thread indefinitely or at the very minimum for time longer than the course of a frame.
 - IO tasks are not CPU intensive and will do minimal processing. Generally will yield readily at any incoming or outbound communication, and thus will only generally be under consistent heavy load only in specific circumstances.
 - Async compute tasks may run for a very long time, across multiple frames, and will generally not yield at any point during a given task's execution. Only under heavy load when a developer explicitly needs it, and can otherwise be used for IO or compute in the general case.

 - [x] Add user-facing APIs for choosing which priority to spawn tasks under.
 - [x] Remove the usages newtypes. Fix up dependent code.
 - [x] Properly set up individual thread groups and their individual prioritization schemes.  
 - [x] Update docs.

---

## Changelog
Changed: Newtypes of `TaskPool` (`ComputeTaskPool`, `AsyncComputeTaskPool`, and `IoTaskPool`) have been replaced with `TaskPool::spawn_as` with the appropriate `TaskGroup`. Thread utilization across these segments has been generally been increased via internal task prioritization. For convenience, `TaskPool::spawn` will always spawn on the compute task group.

## Migration Guide
`ComputeTaskPool`, `AsyncComputeTaskPool`, and `IoTaskPool` have been removed. These individual TaskPools have been merged together, and can be accessed by `Res<TaskPool>`. To spawn a task on a specific segment of the threads, use `TaskPool::spawn_as` with the appropriate `TaskGroup`. 

Before:

```rust
fn system(task_pool: Res<AsyncComputeTaskPool>) {
   task_pool.spawn(async {
       ...
   });
}
```

After:

```rust
fn system(task_pool: Res<TaskPool>) {
   task_pool.spawn(TaskGroup::AsyncCompute, async {
       ...
   });
}
```
pr_comments: I had a slightly different idea on how to combine the task pools. I wanted to give tasks spawned on a scope the highest priority; give tasks spawned onto the task pool a lower priority; and then add a new spawn_blocking function that works like it does in tokio where these tasks are spawned onto a different set of threads. It reuses an idle thread if there are any or spawns a new thread when there aren't any.

> I had a slightly different idea on how to combine the task pools. I wanted to give tasks spawned on a scope the highest priority; give tasks spawned onto the task pool a lower priority; and then add a new spawn_blocking function that works like it does in tokio where these tasks are spawned onto a different set of threads. It reuses an idle thread if there are any or spawns a new thread when there aren't any.

I think the first two parts are still reconcilable with the current proposed approach; however, the problem with  `spawn_blocking` as a general approach is that if a compute thread is idle, you can easily starve out the compute tasks, which is unacceptable in a game engine. Spinning up and down threads is also an overhead we generally want to avoid too, particularly since it can cause even heavier thrashing on the CPU for the other threads.

>  however, the problem with spawn_blocking as a general approach is that if a compute thread is idle, you can easily starve out the compute tasks, which is unacceptable in a game engine.

isn't that a problem with this approach too. If a user starts too many blocking tasks the compute task pool won't have any threads to work with either.

edit: thinking on this more I guess. The approach here prevents the user from running more than `x` blocking tasks at the same time. So the surprise for the user is that when they run too many blocking tasks, they only get `x` running in parallel. Even if they were expecting them to all run in parallel. In the case I suggest, they run as many as they want, but suddenly their game starts stuttering because they've used all the threads.

> isn't that a problem with this approach too. If a user starts too many blocking tasks the compute task pool won't have any threads to work with either.

If and only if they start it as a normal compute task, something that would require `spawn_blocking` should be scheduled to the async compute segment, where under this approach, it'll be delayed until the thread(s) are available.

I just want to say, I am very happy to see this and I think this is the right direction for Bevy.

Using all threads, with internal prioritizing logic for different kinds of tasks, has always seemed like the optimal way to do this. Honestly I was quite surprised when I first learned that Bevy just reserves threads for different task kinds and lets them sit idle when there are no workloads of their kind.

Further, this seems like it would be laying some important groundwork. It should become easier to add more different task classes with different prioritization or scheduling, should we need to do that later.

One example I could think of: we could add a new compute class for the render sub-app tasks. It would make sense, when "actual pipelining" is enabled, to have the render tasks from the previous frame run with higher priority than the compute tasks from the main app update.

This recent change should fix it, though it also doesn't allow for proper prioritization either. It's running the tasks from higher priority task groups, but sometimes it just sits idle. For this to work, we may need to move the distinction into the executor itself.

Thanks to fixes from @hymm the thread utilization of the remaining threads has been fixed.

> > In my mind, all workloads should be able to be scheduled across all logical CPU threads
> 
> This is a good strategy for non-timing sensitive work, but is likely to introduce painful latency in some places. In particular, I expect this strategy will be unacceptable for audio and input management. It is better to have wasted work than delays in some cases.

I've worked on embedded systems running real-time (not real-time operating system, just real-time usage context like audio/video capture and playback in various contexts) multimedia processing tasks with more active processing threads than physical cores / logical threads that leveraged the OS CPU scheduler without problem for audio purposes too. The audio thread would normally be much higher priority as you might expect.

> Thread priority is only on specific platforms. I don't know of a web worker API for it.

That's a good point. But should we aim for lowest common denominator because of one platform, or should we aim for making the most of the different platforms, especially if most do have a thread priority API, and we just have to implement something else for the exceptions that don't? I'd vote for the latter.

> Even then, thread priority is only really useful when you are already using 100% of the CPU and are overcommitted system wide.

I'd probably even want to try without thread priorities first.

> As shown when we erroneously had an extra task pool around, having a non-1:1 correspondence between CPU cores and threads can have a negative impact on perf. An OS level thread context switch is expensive, and we should avoid yielding as much as possible.

I don't mean to be rude in writing this, rather to demonstrate that the argument isn't very strong - I could express something similar but in the other direction that says partitioning available logical threads between different task pools such that some task pools cannot use threads available in other task pools can have a negative impact on performance.

In practice, performance of multi-threaded tasks will vary depending on the number of threads used. Too few and you don't leverage the available processing power. Too many and there's too much contention. But, for example, x264 (a highly optimised H.264 video encoder) _defaults_ to using 1.5x logical threads as this was tested to give the best performance.

I'd like us to try to leverage OS scheduling and show that we _need_ to partition the available logical threads before we do it and prevent tasks from using at least all available logical threads for their processing. Same for whether thread priorities are needed. I'd want to do the simple thing first, test it with different combinations of heavy workloads spawning different amounts of threads, and measure so we can identify the problems we see and come up with solutions to those. Maybe this has already been done and resulted in the current task pool design and I just haven't seen it. From the discussions I've seen, it seems more like there is a fear of overwhelming the CPU and OS scheduler and it causing problems, but this has not been observed in practice. Please tell me, or ideally show me, if I am wrong.

> I've worked on embedded systems running real-time (not real-time operating system, just real-time usage context like audio/video capture and playback in various contexts) multimedia processing tasks with more active processing threads than physical cores / logical threads that leveraged the OS CPU scheduler without problem for audio purposes too. The audio thread would normally be much higher priority as you might expect.

Just to clarify, the proposal here is to still have dedicated threads for lower priority tasks only? Or is the idea to any task run on any thread?

If it's the latter, a counter example is trivially constructed by making an async compute task for every thread spawned that never releases control of the thread back to the task pool. Regardless of how we or the OS prioritizes, those tasks will lock up all of the available threads, and we can't get around that without spawning more threads. In those cases, we *must* defer running lower priority tasks to avoid higher priority starvation. The logical separation *is* bad for perf, that's undeniable, I just question if the alternative is any better. Which leads us to...

If it's the former, I'm concerned about the potential difficult to measure context switching costs. Bevy's built around ECS, meant to minimize the amount of cache misses the CPU incurs. A thread context switch, however infrequent, trashes all of it and forces refetching the entire context from memory. Of course we're already subject to this from the OS and external processes, but I'd really want to avoid incurring this internally wherever possible.

Tested out a suggestion from @hymm to mix both local and global queue stealing and it does seem to improve the results by a bit more. A lot of the more pronounced regressions are better and the gains are bigger.

EDIT: upon deeper inspection, it seems like this change adds a fixed sized overhead when scheduling tasks that scales with the number of threads, but doesn't scale with the number of tasks. You can see this readily in the `empty_systems` benchmark results and compare it against the `overhead_par_iter` ones. It also seems like this overhead is easily eclipsed when there's actual work to be done (see `busy_systems`). Overall I would say this is a workable performance improvement for anything but trivial apps where there's little to nothing to do.

Tested using `sharded-slab` instead of a `Mutex<Slab>` for tracking active tasks, as well as removing it altogether (as suggested before). Removing the active slab removes the only mandatory lock required when spawning tasks, at the cost of potentially delaying followup tasks depending on the OS thread scheduler.

 - `sharded-slab`'s constant overhead is currently higher than a mutex lock on both ends, which takes it out of consideration.
 - Removing the active slab entirely seems to cut the spawning overhead significantly and addresses some of the contention issues. However, it does seem to add additional overhead when waiting for the executor to progress after tasks complete, which seems to be bound by when the OS thread scheduler unparks the associated threads. Probably less of an issue with Bevy in particular since we have a steady stream of incoming tasks that keeps driving the executor.

Found the source of the regression. We were eagerly notifying lower priority task groups if a higher priority one was already notified. This wasn't causing additional contention, but it was causing lower priority threads to be notified around the same time or even before higher priority threads were notified. Said lower priority threads were stealing higher priority tasks (up to half of them in the queue) before the higher priority threads had an opportunity to steal within the group. As higher priority task groups cannot steal from lower priority threads, these tasks, as mentioned above, were getting stuck in smaller thread groups, which was limiting parallelism.

The fix to this was just to avoid notifying lower priority threads if there were available threads in the current priority group that were waiting to be awoken. I also added a cap on the number of tasks that lower priority threads can steal, up to the total number of threads in the lower priority group. This setup prohibits unbounded stealing from higher priority thread groups, but allows stealing just enough to keep all of the local group busy.

Just something to note: this sort of PR, where we have very tricky performance implications due to multithreading, different CPU cores being involved, etc, can be *very sensitive to CPU hardware boost behaviors and such*!

I am worried that there is a high risk of benchmarks being wildly inaccurate (when it comes to judging how much more/less efficient bevy's scheduling has become), due to different thread utilization, causing different boost clocks of different CPUs, etc. The benchmark results may therefore be skewed because of the particular CPU model of the computer they are run on.
